label: Hypothesis Contrary to Fact
argument: If they had just talked to each other instead of ending it over text, they’d definitely be married by now.

label: Appeal to false authority
argument: The HR rep in our building keeps saying that dating coworkers is always a disaster, so I’m going to avoid it. She handles payroll, and if she’s seen enough office drama to say that, she probably knows what she’s talking about.

label: Ecological Fallacy
argument: Our clinic's diabetic patients as a group tend to have high blood pressure, so if Eric has diabetes, he probably has high blood pressure too.

label: Gambler's fallacy
argument: The lab coin has come up tails seven flips straight, so I'm certain the next run will be heads. Random is random, but it can't keep mocking us like this.

label: Appeal to complexity
argument: "That training load is why our striker isn’t recovering well." If I have to read that twice to follow it, then it sounds like a made-up excuse to me.

label: Appeal to Faith
argument: The budget numbers don't add up for another raise right now, but I'm not worried. If you have the right kind of faith in the company, you'll see this bonus is coming.

label: Hasty Generalization
argument: After seeing a few plastic bags snagged in the river near my neighborhood, it’s obvious our city has no real environmental plan. If that’s what the cleanup looks like, the whole program is a joke.

label: Alphabet Soup
argument: If you still think that last call was bad, you’re ignoring the xG, PPDA, VAR, G+A, and B2B numbers, so I’m not going to take your take seriously.

label: Extended Analogy
argument: Ms. Darrow keeps saying chemistry labs are like recipes because the steps have to be followed in order. Recipes are basically the same kind of thing as restaurant operating manuals: they tell people how to produce the same result every time. So her class should be run like a restaurant kitchen, with students judged on speed, uniformity, and how closely they obey instructions rather than on whether they understand the chemistry.

label: Appeal to Definition
argument: The dictionary defines a tablet as a small flat device, so it doesn't make sense to call this foldable laptop a tablet at all. If the shape isn't exactly listed, the label is wrong.

label: Circumstantial Ad Hominem
argument: If the IT lead is pushing this laptop brand, I’m not taking it seriously; his department’s budget is already tied to the vendor’s discounts.

label: Ad Hoc Rescue
argument: A: He said he needed space, but that usually means he’s realizing the relationship matters and he’s just sorting out his feelings. B: So you think the silence is actually a good sign? A: Exactly, because people pull away when they’re trying not to rush back too soon.

label: Retrogressive Causation
argument: People are saying homework is stressing everyone out, but the best way to fix that is to assign more homework so students can get over the stress from homework faster.

label: Complex question fallacy
argument: Did your manager ever explain why your team gets rewarded for missing deadlines?

label: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
argument: I looked at the app reviews, and five-star ratings are clustered around phones launched in spring. That’s enough for me to say spring releases are just better tech.

label: Inflation of Conflict
argument: If one pastor says the prayer group helps and another says it's just a habit, then what are we supposed to believe? People who study religion clearly don't know enough for any real answer.

label: Proving Nonexistence
argument: “We shouldn’t tell visitors the relic has healing power when there’s no good evidence it has ever healed anyone.” “Unless you can prove there is no healing power in it at all, you have no grounds for doubting what the church says about it.”

label: Circular Reasoning
argument: That team is clearly the best in the league because they win so much, and they win so much because they’re the best in the league.

label: Argument from Silence
argument: I asked three times whether your dog bit the neighbor’s kid, and you just stared at the floor. That tells me your dog did it.

label: Proof Surrogate
argument: Stop acting like the bank fees are normal; the app showing my balance dropping every week is all the proof you need that they’re draining us on purpose.

label: Existential Fallacy
argument: A: Every runner on the relay team is a varsity athlete. B: And every varsity athlete is cleared for the 5K trial. So some runners on the relay team are definitely cleared for the 5K trial.

label: Appeal to Intuition
argument: If the new raid strategy is so good, why does it still feel wrong when I watch it? We should stick with the old one, because my instincts say the new setup isn't the way this game is meant to be played.

label: Appeal to common sense
argument: "A higher sensitivity is always better in shooters." That's just common sense if you've played anything competitive. If your aim is good, the faster setting clearly makes you better.

label: Appeal to Fear
argument: We need the new surveillance bill because if we don't pass it, the city will be helpless the next time something goes wrong on the subway, and nobody wants to be the one blamed when panic breaks out.

label: Amazing familiarity
argument: A: “The clinic says my headaches are probably from stress.” B: They say that because they know your blood pressure spikes every night after you lie awake checking your phone, and the nurse who called you back has already marked it as a pattern.

label: Fantasy Projection
argument: "It was just a dumb comedy show." No, it was cruel, and if you didn’t feel how insulting that scene was, you’re ignoring what was right in front of you.

label: Argumentum Ad Criminum
argument: I know Cara says daycare helps kids learn to share, but she’s paying for the fancy private center downtown, so I’m not buying her take. If she were right, she wouldn’t need to spend that much to prove it.

label: Pragmatic Fallacy
argument: Our manager’s new check-in routine has people hitting deadlines more consistently, so I’m convinced it’s the right way to measure productivity. If a method gets better results, that’s evidence the method reflects the truth.

label: Accident
argument: You keep saying science changes its mind, but that’s exactly why we should treat every established rule as fixed once it’s taught. If it’s in a textbook, it must hold in every case.

label: Appeal to Possibility
argument: "Maybe the quiz was just a bad day," but that means the grade could be inflated, so I shouldn't trust it for the final average.

label: Base Rate Fallacy
argument: You can keep saying the results are consistent with the normal error rate, but this sample is different because the lab tech looked nervous and the equipment was new. That’s why I’m sure the finding is real and not just one of those typical false alarms.

label: Denying the correlative
argument: You said the concert is either worth the ticket price or it isn't. Honestly, I think it's more about who went with us and what mood you were in, so the price question doesn't really decide anything.
